Chapter 2: Setting Out—The First Days on the Open Sea.
The first days drifting on the raft? They were humbling, to say the least. The ocean—well, it doesn’t coddle anyone. That raft, which felt so solid back on shore, now groaned and shifted with every wave. The crew found themselves moving slowly, carefully, learning how to balance their weight and trust this odd, floating world beneath them.
Pretty soon, life out there settled into its own rhythm. There were plenty of chores—checking the ropes, adjusting the sail, always keeping an eye out for land or danger. Meals were nothing fancy: just dried food, or whatever the ocean happened to offer. The sun beat down during the day, relentless and hot. And when night fell, the cold and damp crept in. They’d catch sleep in short snatches, often woken by the sound of water slapping against the logs.
In the beginning, everyone felt exposed, almost fragile. The Pacific just stretched on and on, a vast blue emptiness, and the raft felt tiny in comparison. Doubts crept in, especially on those days when the horizon showed nothing but sky and the wind seemed to disappear. Yet, bit by bit, the crew began to adapt. They learned to read the waves, to sense even the smallest changes in the wind, and to find comfort in the small routines of daily life.
Then, there were the moments of wonder. One evening, as the sun dipped low, the sky exploded with stars. The ocean itself shimmered, glowing with the light of a thousand tiny creatures. For a moment, everyone just stared, reminded that the world is so much bigger—and more mysterious—than any map can capture. They felt small, sure, but also connected to something ancient and vast. That feeling? It would come back to them, again and again, throughout their journey.
Of course, it wasn’t all awe and discovery. The raft was tricky to steer, and the currents liked to drag them off course. Supplies had to be watched closely, rationed out with care. Nothing ever seemed to go as quickly as planned. But the crew found ways to cope. They swapped stories, sang songs, and managed to laugh at the little mishaps that came with life at sea.
Then, one day, a sudden squall rolled in and put them to the test. The wind screamed, waves crashed over the raft, drenching everything and threatening to pull the logs apart. The men sprang into action—tightening ropes, bailing water, hands raw and nerves stretched thin. When the storm finally eased, they were soaked and exhausted. But they were still together. The raft had survived, and so had their spirit.
In the hush that followed, something shifted. The journey wasn’t just about reaching some distant shore—it was about endurance. The ocean demanded respect, and the crew learned to give it. They started to trust the raft, and each other, in ways words couldn’t quite capture. What began as an experiment was turning into a real test of patience, character, and faith.
As days blended into weeks, the men found a sort of uneasy peace. The world they’d left behind felt far away, almost like a dream. Ahead of them? Only the unknown, and the hope that the winds and currents would eventually carry them where they needed to go.
